name: Subperiosteal facelift

card.summary: A midface lift done beneath the periosteum, often endoscopically, that repositions cheek tissue vertically; documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.
card.note: Wikipedia notes longer postoperative swelling; nerve anatomy around the cheekbone and temple is a recognized surgical concern.

quick.overview:
A subperiosteal facelift frees the soft tissue of the cheek and midface from the facial bones by working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering bone. The tissue is then repositioned, mainly in an upward direction, to address flattened cheeks and deep nasolabial folds.

Surgeons in the 1990s described open and endoscopic versions, with the endoscopic approach using small incisions hidden in the hair. Available evidence is surgeon-reported series rather than randomized trials.
quick.mechanism: Dissection lifts soft tissue off bone so the whole mask of the face can be moved as a unit and fixed higher. Endoscopes let surgeons see the deep plane through short incisions.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states the technique causes longer postoperative swelling than some alternatives. Anatomical studies highlight nerves in the cheekbone and temple region, such as the zygomaticotemporal nerve, whose injury can cause numbness or pain. General facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury and scarring.

lead: A subperiosteal facelift is a surgical technique in which the soft tissues of the face are lifted completely off the underlying bone by dissecting beneath the periosteum, then repositioned. It is used to address deep nasolabial folds and sagging cheeks and is often combined with other techniques.[1]

A 1995 report by endoscopic surgeons describes it as particularly suited to remodeling the central third of the face, and states that the endoscope allows upper-face or total-face rejuvenation without incisional scars, while making deep dissection safer and more accurate.[2] A companion 1995 article describes open and endoscopic approaches and states the endoscopic procedure alone is indicated for mild aging (grade I rhytidosis), and in men with alopecia in whom a coronal incision is a problem, where it may be combined with neck surgery.[3]

Evidence consists of surgeon-reported series and anatomical studies; no randomized comparison with other facelifts was found.[2][3] The procedure was first described in French plastic surgery in the 1980s as the mask lift, and a 2024 French article presents the technique again as still having a place in practice, alone for aesthetic purposes or combined with reconstructive surgery.[12][15] In looksmaxxing communities it belongs to hardmaxxing, in discussions of midface and cheek restructuring.

paras: In the subperiosteal approach, soft tissue is released from the bone, including retaining attachments, and repositioned in a vertical direction.[1][2] Wikipedia describes it as used across age groups and as causing longer postoperative swelling.[1]
Related Chinese and French reports from the 1990s and 2000 describe combined or modified subperiosteal facelifts and a so-called mask lift, reflecting its spread internationally.[4][5][6]

The French surgeon who introduced the mask lift described the facial mask as everything lying on the skeleton: periosteum, deep fat, the superficial musculo-aponeurotic layer and skin. The periosteum is the layer between the bones that shape the face and the more mobile tissues above, and a complete subperiosteal release of the cheekbones, zygomatic arches and orbital margins is described as the key to an effective lift.[15] The release can be done through a coronal incision across the scalp, or started through a short incision inside the mouth.[15] The same article notes that the coronal approach can also be used to remodel the orbital rims and to harvest bone grafts to reinforce the glabella, cheekbones and nasolabial folds.[15]

Because the lift moves the deep tissue plane in an upward direction, proponents of the technique describe it as restoring the position of cheek fat that has descended, rather than pulling the skin sideways. A later review of surgical approaches around the eye describes the bicoronal incision as a classic craniofacial route used for tumors, fractures and reconstruction, which is the setting in which subperiosteal dissection was first routine.[16]

Subperiosteal dissection of the face was developed in craniofacial surgery; Wikipedia credits Paul Tessier with using subperiosteal dissection through a coronal incision and with showing in 1979 that undermining the orbital rims allowed better elevation of soft tissue and eyebrows.[1] In the mid-1990s, endoscopic versions were published, aiming to avoid long incisions.[2][3] A 1998 article asked whether the evolution from endoscopic to mini-invasive facelift was a logical progression.[7]

Wikipedia's survey of facelift history places Tessier's subperiosteal work in the deep plane period (1980 to 1991), after the skin-only era (1900 to 1970) and the SMAS era of the 1970s, in which Tord Skoog's subfacial dissection (1974) and the SMAS description by Mitz and Peyronie (1976) were introduced.[1] A French surgeon reported 130 mask lift cases since 1981 in a 1989 paper, calling the method a new approach to the aging face.[14] Chinese surgeons began applying video endoscopy to facial rejuvenation in July 1995 and described 15 subperiosteal operations combined with liposuction of the submandibular area and nasolabial fold, reporting small incisions, less edema, less numbness and no hair loss.[5] Wikipedia also records a 1998 review of 200 subperiosteal facelifts by Heinrichs and Kaidi.[1]

A 1995 French clinical review describes video endoscopy as having reduced the size of incisions in forehead and mask lifts, and states that the indications for the mask lift, which aims at a more radical change of the upper and middle thirds of the face, should be decided cautiously given the psychological side.[17]

Wikipedia lists the subperiosteal facelift among the main variants alongside the SMAS facelift, the deep-plane facelift (which moves skin and soft tissue with the malar fat pad as one unit after releasing retaining ligaments), the composite facelift described by Hamra in 1992 and the minimal-access cranial suspension (MACS) lift.[1] It states that the subperiosteal approach is associated with a longer period of facial swelling than other lifts, while skin-only lifts are associated with quicker recovery.[1] The deep-plane approach is described as technically demanding because it runs closer to facial nerve branches.[1]

A cadaver study of the zygomaticotemporal nerve notes that its injury causes paresthesia in the area it supplies and that it can be entrapped during procedures including endoscopic subperiosteal facelift.[8] A separate anatomical report studies foramina on the zygomatic bone for their clinical significance.[9]
For facelifts generally, complications include hematoma, facial or sensory nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss at incisions.[1]

Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common facelift complication, usually appearing within the first 24 hours, and names the greater auricular nerve as the most commonly injured sensory nerve and the facial nerve as the most commonly injured motor nerve. Smoking is reported to raise skin necrosis risk about twelvefold, and permanent hair loss near temporal incisions is possible.[1]

A study of 50 dry skulls from southern India measured the number and position of the small foramina of the zygomatic bone, which carry the nerves and vessels that subperiosteal dissection passes near, and found the number varied from none to four per side.[9]

Human data are surgeon-reported. The 1995 reports describe indications and technique rather than controlled outcomes.[2][3] A 2006 Brazilian paper summarizes a 5-year experience with the technique.[10] Temporal hollowing augmentation with methyl methacrylate has been described as a related but separate procedure for temple volume.[11] No randomized trials comparing subperiosteal with other facelift techniques were found. The 1989 mask lift series reported 130 cases.[14] A 15-patient Chinese endoscopic series reported small incisions, less edema, less numbness and no hair loss.[5] A 2011 report describes filling temple hollows with methyl methacrylate placed beneath the temporalis muscle in people who had undergone subperiosteal facelift dissection, with the authors calling the technique reliable, durable and relatively free of complications.[11]

Within hardmaxxing, the subperiosteal facelift is grouped with other midface and cheek procedures, for people who want to change flat or descended cheeks through surgery. Published literature on the operation itself comes from plastic surgeons rather than from community sources.

angle.text: The subperiosteal facelift is a surgical route to a lifted midface: the cheek tissue is released from the cheekbone and fixed higher, which is how people use it to restore cheek fullness and soften the lines running from nose to mouth. Because it works on the central third of the face, it is discussed in hardmaxxing as a way to change midface projection and eye-to-cheek balance.
